query: For high-entropy-alloy multilayer protective coatings, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation? Specify what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, the expected observations relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy-alloy multilayer protective coatings, engineering the interfaces to have a controlled misfit in combination with ultrathin graphene-like barriers will impede the transmission of dislocations between layers, thereby reducing time-dependent plastic deformation (creep) under service conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy-alloy multilayer coatings with standard interfacial characteristics exhibiting time-dependent plastic deformation under stress and temperature.
generation.intervention: Introduce engineered interfacial misfit and incorporate ultrathin graphene-like barrier layers at the coating interfaces.
generation.conditions: Tested under elevated temperatures and sustained mechanical stress (creep conditions) where dislocation slip and grain boundary sliding become active.
generation.structural_mediator: The ultrathin graphene-like barrier physically blocks dislocation transfer across interfaces, while the engineered interfacial misfit promotes coherency stresses that further hinder dislocation nucleation and motion.
generation.mechanism: The combination of interfacial misfit-induced stress fields and the high elastic modulus of graphene barriers operates to obstruct the movement and pile-up of dislocations. This dual barrier mechanism reduces the propagation of plastic deformation through the multilayer structure, slowing the creep process.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline multilayer coating without the graphene-like barrier and engineered misfit, the modified coating will exhibit a significantly lower creep rate and reduced accumulation of plastic strain, as evidenced by lower dislocation densities observed at interfaces.
generation.baseline: Multilayer HEA protective coatings designed without the engineered interfacial misfit and without graphene-like barrier layers.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected under conditions typical for high-temperature, stress-driven creep tests (e.g., intermediate temperatures up to ~600°C and applied stresses where dislocation activity and grain boundary sliding dominate). The benefits may diminish if the applied conditions exceed the stability range of the graphene barrier or if other failure modes (e.g., oxidation) become operative.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of creep rate reduction and the relative contribution of the interfacial misfit versus the graphene barrier are not fully quantified and may depend on the specifics of barrier thickness, misfit magnitude, and operating conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of multilayer HEA coatings: one set with the engineered interfacial misfit and integrated ultrathin graphene-like barrier layers (intervention group) and one set with standard interfaces (control group). Subject both sets to identical creep testing conditions at elevated temperatures and applied stresses. Utilize electron microscopy and diffraction techniques to monitor dislocation activity and interface integrity over time.
measurements: Creep rate (plastic strain vs time) under constant load and temperature.
Dislocation density and distribution at and across the interfaces using TEM and/or high-resolution SEM.
Mechanical testing to quantify yield strength and strain hardening behavior.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coatings with the engineered interfaces and graphene barriers do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in creep rate and dislocation density compared to the control coatings under identical testing conditions, then the hypothesis that the intervention impedes time-dependent plastic deformation is falsified.

In this paper, MD simulations are conducted to systematically investigate the creep behavior of HESAs under varying stress, temperature, γ/γ′ lattice misfit, and γ′ volume fraction. The creep mechanism and the critical creep resistance factors are explored. The main conclusions are summarized as follows: The creep behavior of both HESAs and HEAs is strongly influenced by stress and temperature, and their combined effect governs the rate of atomic rearrangement during deformation. As these parameters increase, the creep rate accelerates rapidly due to enhanced diffusion and easier activation of deformation carriers. Temperature plays a particularly dominant role, as high thermal energy significantly facilitates atomic mobility, vacancy migration, and interface-mediated processes. Compared with HEAs, HESAs consistently exhibit lower creep strain under identical conditions, and the difference becomes more pronounced at higher stress–temperature combinations, highlighting the intrinsic microstructural advantages of γ/γ′-strengthened systems.

A clear transition in creep mechanisms is observed, evolving from diffusion-dominated deformation at low stresses to dislocation nucleation, glide, and interaction at intermediate conditions, and ultimately to stress-induced phase transformation at higher stresses and temperatures. This progression is corroborated by atomic-scale structural evolution and steady-state creep theory. Under identical conditions, HESAs show markedly superior creep resistance to HEAs, mainly due to the strong blocking effect of γ/γ′ interfaces on dislocation motion and atomic transport. Both the γ/γ′ lattice misfit and γ′ volume fraction exert a critical influence on creep resistance. The relationship between misfit magnitude and creep behavior is non-monotonic: moderate negative misfit enhances interfacial coherency and stabilizes the microstructure, thereby improving creep resistance, whereas excessively large misfit increases interfacial strain energy and deteriorates performance. A negative misfit is generally more effective in resisting creep because it strengthens the γ/γ′ interface and reduces dislocation transmissibility. The tensile creep behavior of an equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy was systematically investigated over an intermediate temperature range (500–600 °C) and applied stress (140–400 MPa). The alloy exhibited a stress-dependent transition from a low-stress region (LSR-region I) to a high-stress region (HSR-region II). The LSR was characterized by a stress exponent of 5 to 6 and an average activation energy of 268 kJ mol−1, whereas the HSR showed much higher corresponding values of 8.9–14 and 380 kJ mol−1. Microstructural examinations on the deformed samples revealed remarkable dynamic recrystallization at higher stress levels. Dislocation jogging and tangling configurations were frequently observed in LSR and HSR at 550 and 600 °C, respectively. Moreover, dynamic precipitates identified as M23C6 or a Cr-rich σ phase were formed along grain boundaries in HSR. Recently, Ding et al. synthesized FCC CoCrFeNiPd and CoCrFeNiMn HEAs. The former exhibited a higher yield strength than the latter with comparable tensile ductility. They proposed that the essential difference between these two HEAs was associated with atomic segregation and short-range ordering (SRO); both were enhanced in CoCrFeNiPd, as compared with CoCrFeNiMn. The idea was that SRO tends to create resistance to deformation/slip, leading to larger dislocation glide resistance in the more ordered CoCrFeNiPd than in CoCrFeNiMn HEAs. Theoretical work by Yin et al. suggested that the strengthening was due mainly to the large atomic/misfit volume of Pd in CoCrFeNi. Ma et al. identified a number of unusual features associated with dislocations/slips in HEAs that were related to lattice distortion and/or local chemical order. SRO also occurs in medium-entropy alloys (MEAs). The atomic structure of a CoCrNi MEA indicates that Cr favors Ni and Co neighbors, reducing the electrical and thermal conductivities and increasing the stacking-fault energies and hardness.

As the strain was up to 16.2%, a parallel dislocation was initiated and eventually blocked by the monolayer graphene. No obvious step was found in graphene after obstructing several dislocation activities, which was a result of a ~1 TPa measured modulus in monolayer graphene [], restricting dislocation activities within the upper part of the HEA/graphene composites and, therefore, effectively strengthening the HEA matrix. It is worth mentioning that mirror-like dislocation emission and motion were found after encountering the graphene barrier. Analogous to stimulated emission in laser theory, which has been theoretically and experimentally proved in Cu and Ti alloys [,], the dislocation slip can be promoted to the next layer to sustain the deformation and decrease the stress concentration near the interface. In this case, such stimulated slip endows dislocation storage near the interface and in the upper part of HEA inner grains during continuous deformation.

reading.lever: Combine multilayer coatings with engineered interfacial misfit and ultrathin graphene-like barriers to block dislocation transfer.
reading.why: This combined approach, proven in γ/γ′ systems and HEA/graphene composites, directly targets time-dependent plastic deformation in multilayer protective coatings.
